message.content:
### Tenant Rights in Texas (as of 2024) | Area | What You’re Entitled To | Key Points | |------|------------------------|------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Must be returned within 30 days after you move out (unless you and the landlord agree otherwise).
• Landlord may keep up to one month’s rent for damages beyond normal wear & tear. | • Landlord must provide an itemized list of deductions.
• If the landlord fails to return the deposit or itemize deductions, you can sue for the full amount plus damages. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must maintain the premises in a safe, livable condition (e.g., plumbing, heating, electrical, structural integrity). | • If the landlord fails to fix major problems, you can withhold rent, repair & deduct, or terminate the lease. | | **Notice Requirements** | • For non‑payment of rent: 3‑day notice to pay or vacate.
• For lease termination: 30‑day notice if you’re on a month‑to‑month lease; 60‑day notice if you’re on a fixed‑term lease. | • Notice must be in writing and delivered personally or by mail. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must file a **Petition for Eviction** in the county court.
• Court will issue a **Writ of Possession** if you fail to comply. | • You have the right to contest the eviction in court. | | **Rent Increases** | • No statutory limit on how much a landlord can raise rent, but it must be in writing and given at least 30 days’ notice. | • For month‑to‑month tenants, a 30‑day notice is required. | | **Discrimination** | • Landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income (e.g., public assistance). | • This is protected under the Texas Fair Housing Act and federal law. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • You have the right to live without unreasonable interference from the landlord or other tenants. | • Landlord must respect your privacy and not enter without proper notice (usually 24 hours). | | **Repair & Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to fix a major problem, you may repair it yourself and deduct the cost from your rent. | • You must keep receipts and notify the landlord in writing. | | **Lease Terms** | • The lease is a binding contract.
• Landlord cannot unilaterally change terms without your consent. | • Any changes must be documented in writing. | | **Subletting & Assignment** | • Many leases allow subletting or assignment with landlord’s written consent. | • If the lease prohibits it, you must obtain permission or risk breach. | | **Utilities** | • Landlord must provide essential utilities (water, heat, electricity) unless otherwise specified. | • If utilities are not provided, you may be entitled to a rent reduction. | | **Legal Remedies** | • You can sue for unpaid rent, damages, or breach of contract.
• Small claims court handles disputes up to $20,000. | • Keep all documentation (receipts, emails, text messages). | --- #### How to Protect Your Rights 1. **Read Your Lease Carefully** – Understand every clause, especially those about deposits, repairs, and notice periods. 2. **Document Everything** – Keep copies of all communications, receipts, and photos of any damage or maintenance issues. 3. **Use Written Notices** – Send notices via certified mail or email with read receipts to establish proof of delivery. 4. **Know the Local Ordinances** – Some cities (e.g., Austin, Dallas) have additional tenant protections beyond state law. 5. **Seek Legal Aid** – If you face eviction or a dispute, consult a local attorney or tenant advocacy group. --- #### Useful Resources | Resource | What It Offers | |----------|----------------| | **Texas Attorney General – Consumer Protection Division** | Information on landlord‑tenant laws, complaint filing. | | **Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA)** | Guidance on fair housing and rental assistance. | | **Local Legal Aid Societies** | Free or low‑cost legal advice for tenants. | | **Texas Tenants’ Association** | Advocacy, educational materials, and support groups. | | **Small Claims Court** | Quick resolution for disputes under $20,000. | --- **Bottom Line:** As a Texas tenant, you have the right to a safe, habitable home, timely return of your security deposit, proper notice before eviction or lease changes, and protection against discrimination. If your landlord violates these rights, you have legal avenues to seek remedy—often starting with written communication and, if necessary, court action.
